Our Work maps each task to its analytical method
Task 1: four indicators described, K-means clusters countries

Evaluation lists strengths and weaknesses with model-level detail
Further discussion proposes data expansion and policy tailoring
Memorandum distills findings into ITU summit recommendations

main_argument_chains.claim: Countries cluster into three risk tiers based on NCSI and legal measures, with the Purple Cluster showing the strongest cybersecurity posture.
support_steps: Select four cybersecurity indicators from public databases
Apply K-means with K=3 validated by elbow and silhouette
Characterize each cluster by indicator means
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Cluster membership determines which countries need policy intervention.

main_argument_chains.claim: Data Protection, Network Operator Obligations, and Cross-Border Data Flow policies significantly reduce cybercrime rates, while Criminal Legislation, Infrastructure Protection, and Emergency Response do not.
support_steps: Categorize policies into six themes via LDA
Select experimental and control country groups per theme
Fit DID regression for each theme
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Three effective themes form the basis of memo recommendations; three ineffective themes are flagged for improvement.

main_argument_chains.claim: Internet Penetration Rate has the strongest average correlation (MIC 0.849) with cybercrime cases, while GDP has the weakest (0.32).
support_steps: Compute MIC values for each country-variable pair
Fit stepwise regression on factor scores
Rank variables by average MIC across countries
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Demographic findings guide policy tailoring: countries with high internet penetration need stronger data protection.

warnings.warning: Last-pass warning: The DID model specification is referenced in prose ("The DID model was formulated as follows") but the actual equation is on a raster-only page region. The text layer at this point gives only the prose introduction, not the equation itself.

Last-pass warning: Table 3 (Data Protection OLS) reports Diff-in-Diff coefficient 0.708 with p=0.022, but the Table 4 (Network Operators OLS on page 17) reports coefficient 0.31 with p=0.01. The text refers to six policy themes, but only three are reported with full OLS tables. The other three themes are reported in prose only with no tabular support.

Last-pass warning: The experimental group for each policy theme consists of only 1-2 countries. With such small treatment groups, the DID estimates are vulnerable to idiosyncratic shocks and the standard errors may be unreliable. The paper does not discuss small-sample limitations.
Last-pass warning: K-means clustering uses only NCSI and Legal Measures as features. CEI and Reporting Rate are described in the same section but excluded from clustering without explanation.

Last-pass warning: The factor analysis variable labels (GNC, GDG, SETE, AMBS, IPR) are used without defining what each abbreviation stands for. Only IPR (Internet Penetration Rate) and AMBS (Active Mobile-Broadband Subscriptions) are inferable from context; the others are ambiguous.

Last-pass warning: MIC values are computed per country-variable pair, but the text does not state which time period or which aggregation (annual average, cumulative) the cybercrime case count covers. The unit of Y in the heatmap is unstated.

Last-pass warning: The paper states "we meticulously selected countries" for each policy group but never lists all selected countries. Only a few are named (Australia, Ireland, UK, New Zealand, Singapore). The full group composition is unavailable for replication.

Last-pass warning: Reporting rates are given in scientific notation (2.24e-05) without explaining whether the denominator is population, internet users, or incidents. The rate units differ by several orders of magnitude from what percentages would produce, suggesting a per-capita rate, but this is never stated.

Last-pass warning: The DID design requires parallel trends between treatment and control groups. The paper does not present a parallel-trends test or visual check. With only 1-2 countries per group, such a test would have very low power.

Last-pass warning: The memo recommends "clarifying cross-border data flow rules" but the DID analysis for this theme (page 17) does not report significance clearly. The connection between the statistical finding and the recommendation is not traceable.
